Lab 12

Chess pawn

Copy a real chess pawn from a photo: one cylinder, built up ring by ring with four keys, G, Z, E and S.

Start the lab

Rendered in Blender by following the steps in this lab.

Today

We are learning

how a 3D modeller copies a real object from a photo: one cylinder, built up ring by ring with four keys, G, Z, E and S, and typed numbers that make every ring exact.

You need Blender 4.1 or newer (this lab was built in 5.2), a mouse with a scroll wheel and a middle button (laptop trackpad? see this fix), and about two lessons. Save your file as Lab12_Pawn_YourName.blend.

You’ve got it when you can

  • put a reference photo beside your model in an Image Editor
  • place an object exactly with the sidebar and check it from the front
  • select a loop with Alt+click in Edge select
  • move with G and Z, extrude with E and scale with S, by typed numbers, and say what a scale number does
  • close a shape with M › At Center, smooth it and give it a material

The plan

Five parts. Each one ends with a picture of what your pawn should look like.

  1. Part 1The photo beside the modelSteps 1–5
  2. Part 2The baseSteps 6–11
  3. Part 3Stem and collarSteps 12–14
  4. Part 4The headSteps 15–17
  5. Part 5Finish and hand inSteps 18–20

One cylinder, ring by ring

Look at a chess pawn from the side and it is a stack of circles: wide at the bottom, thin in the stem, a disc for the collar, a ball on top. That is how you build it. You select the top of a cylinder once, then keep doing two things: E pulls a new ring up out of the top, and S makes that ring wider or narrower. G with Z moves it up or down. Every number is typed, so your pawn comes out exactly like the plan.

Word bank — open this if a word in the steps is new
Area
One rectangle of the Blender window. Each area shows one editor; you can split an area in two.
Image Editor
The editor that shows pictures. Here it holds the reference photo.
Reference photo
A picture of the real object, kept on screen to copy from.
Object Mode / Edit Mode
Object Mode moves whole objects; Edit Mode changes the shape. Tab swaps between them.
Edge select (2)
In Edit Mode, clicks pick edges. 1 picks corners (vertices), 3 picks faces.
Loop (Alt+click)
A whole ring of edges, selected with one Alt+click.
G (grab)
Move what is selected. Followed by Z: move it only up and down.
E (extrude)
Pull new geometry out of the selection. On the top face: a new ring.
S (scale)
Make the selection bigger or smaller. The typed number is a multiplier: 0.9 means 0.9 times as wide.
Merge (M › At Center)
Squash all the selected corners into one point in their middle.
Shade Auto Smooth
Smooth shading on curves, sharp shading where faces meet at more than 30°.
Material Preview
The shading mode (Z) that shows colours and shine.

Part 1

The photo beside the model

Tools: File › New, View › Area › Vertical Split, the Editor Type menu, the Image Editor’s Open.

A modeller copying a real object keeps a photo of it on screen the whole time and keeps looking from one to the other. Five steps put the photo on the left and an empty 3D view on the right.

How the steps work

Each step has a Where line (which part of the Blender window to look at), a Watch animation of the step (pause it, drag the slider, or use the arrow buttons to go one move at a time), and a Do this list of the same moves as a, b, c. Keys in a row like G Z -1.8 Enter are pressed one after another, not together; keys joined with a plus, like Shift+A, are held together. A gold outline in a drawing marks a box you type into; Blender itself keeps it grey.

  1. Start fresh and save

    The File menu at the very top-left of the Blender window.

    Do this:

    1. a
      File › New › General. A fresh scene: a cube, a camera and a light.
    2. b
      File › Save As. Open your Lab 12 folder (make one if you need to), type Lab12_Pawn_YourName and click Save Blender File.
    3. c
      From now on press Ctrl+S every few steps.

    You should now see: the window title shows your file name.

    Why save first?

    Once the file has a name, saving is one key. Ctrl+S takes a second; redoing twenty steps takes a lesson.

  2. Split the window in two

    The 3D Viewport’s own header (the strip along its top), its View menu. Not the File menu at the very top.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Hover the 3D Viewport. In its header: View › Area › Vertical Split.
    2. b
      A line follows the mouse. Move it to the middle of the screen and click.

    You should now see: two 3D Viewports side by side, each with its own header.

    Can I drag instead?

    Yes: point at the top-left corner of the 3D Viewport until the cursor turns into a cross, then drag to the right. The menu is easier to get right first time. Split it the wrong way (one above the other)? Hover the extra half, View › Area › Close Area, and try again.

  3. Turn the left half into an Image Editor

    The left half’s header: the small button at its very left end (the Editor Type button).

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click the Editor Type button at the very left of the left half’s header.
    2. b
      In the General column click Image Editor.

    You should now see: the left half goes dark, with New and Open in its header.

    What is an editor?

    Every area of the Blender window shows one editor, and the button at the left of its header changes which. The 3D Viewport, the Outliner and the Properties editor are all just areas showing different editors.

  4. Load the photo

    This page (the download button), then the Image Editor’s header and the file browser it opens.

    The reference photo. A Staunton-style pawn on a wooden board, from the front.

    Download the pawn photo

    Save it as pawn_reference.jpg in your Lab 12 folder.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click Download the pawn photo above and save it in your Lab 12 folder.
    2. b
      In Blender, hover the Image Editor and click Open in its header (or Image › Open, or Alt+O).
    3. c
      In the file browser go to your Lab 12 folder, click pawn_reference.jpg, then Open Image.
    4. d
      The photo opens at full size, too big to see. Hover it and press Home: it fits the half.

    You should now see: the pawn photo filling the left half.

    Why not File › Open?

    File › Open opens .blend files: it would replace your whole scene, and it does not even list pictures. A picture goes in through the Image Editor’s own Open.

  5. Clear the 3D side

    The right half. Blender sends every key to the half the mouse is over.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Move the mouse over the right half. Press A: the cube, the camera and the light all turn orange.
    2. b
      Press X, then click Delete.

    You should now see: an empty grid on the right, the photo on the left.

    Why does it matter where the mouse is?

    Every key goes to the area under the mouse. Press A over the photo and nothing happens to your objects. Keep the mouse on the right half for the rest of the lab.

End of Part 1. Ctrl+S.

Part 2

The base

Tools: Shift+A, the N sidebar, Tab, Edge select (2), Alt+click, and the four moves: G Z, E, S, E then S.

A cylinder becomes the whole pawn. Its top face is selected once, in Step 8, and stays selected for the rest of the lab: every move changes the top, and every E makes a new top. Watch the photo as you go: base, stem, collar, head.

  1. Add a cylinder

    The right half. Shift+A opens the Add menu where the mouse is.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Mouse over the right half: Shift+A › Mesh › Cylinder.
    2. b
      Bottom-left, the Add Cylinder panel: leave it as it is. Vertices 32, Radius 1 m, Depth 2 m.

    You should now see: a cylinder at the centre of the grid, half of it below the floor, with an orange outline.

    Why do these numbers matter?

    Every number in this lab is worked out from this cylinder: 1 m from the middle to the edge, 2 m tall, 32 sides. A different radius gives a bigger or smaller pawn of the same shape; more sides make it smoother, fewer make it blockier.

  2. Stand it on the grid

    The N sidebar, Item tab; then the front view.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Mouse over the right half, press N. In the Item tab click Location Z, type 1, Enter.
    2. b
      Numpad 1: the front view. The bottom of the cylinder sits exactly on the red line.
    3. c
      N again hides the sidebar. Orbit (drag with the middle mouse button) until you look down on the top of the cylinder.

    You should now see: the cylinder standing on the grid, its top 2 m up.

    Why Location Z 1?

    The cylinder grows out from its middle, so it starts from -1 m to 1 m. Lifting the middle to 1 m puts the bottom at 0: on the floor, like a pawn on a board.

  3. Select the top

    The left end of the 3D view’s header: the mode menu and the three select buttons beside it.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Tab: Edit Mode. The whole cylinder turns orange (a new object starts with everything selected).
    2. b
      Press 2 for Edge select (or click the middle one of the three buttons next to Edit Mode).
    3. c
      Hold Alt and click the middle of the top face. Only the circle round the top and the top face stay orange.

    You should now see: an orange top and grey sides.

    What did Alt+click do?

    Alt+click selects a whole loop: every edge in a ring. Round the top of a cylinder that ring is the top circle, and when all of a face’s edges are selected Blender selects the face too. From now on every E leaves the newest top selected, so you never have to select again.

Ring builder

The whole pawn, move by move: 34 moves in Steps 9 to 17. Step through them to see what each number does before you type it.

0 / 34

  1. Squash it into a disc

    The right half (3D view), keys only. The mouse can be anywhere over it; the typed number decides the size. Scroll the wheel to zoom in on it if you like.

    Do this:

    1. a
      G Z -1.8 Enter. G grabs (moves), Z locks the move to straight up and down, -1.8 is how far: minus means down.

    You should now see: a flat disc 0.2 m thick (2 − 1.8), its top still orange.

    Why type the number?

    G on its own makes the top follow the mouse, and every pawn would come out different. Typing the number makes it exact: the mouse position no longer matters, only the number.

  2. A sloped edge, then a step

    The right half (3D view), keys only. The mouse can be anywhere over it; the typed number decides the size.

    Do this:

    1. a
      E 0.08 Enter, then S 0.92 Enter. A new ring 0.08 m higher, narrowed to 0.92 of its width: a sloped edge.
    2. b
      E, then straight away S 0.92 Enter. A flat step inwards.

    You should now see: the disc with a bevelled top edge and a narrower step on top of it.

    What does S 0.92 mean?

    Multiply the width by 0.92. The top circle is 1 m from the middle: 1 × 0.92 = 0.92 m. The step: 0.92 × 0.92 = 0.846 m. S always means “times the width it has now”: numbers below 1 shrink it, numbers above 1 widen it.

  3. The ring

    The right half (3D view), keys only. The mouse can be anywhere over it; the typed number decides the size.

    Do this:

    1. a
      E 0.1 Enter, then S 1.05 Enter. The ring widens a little as it rises.
    2. b
      E 0.1 Enter, then S 0.92 Enter. And tucks back in.

    You should now see: a rounded ring sitting on the base, like the bottom of the photo’s pawn.

    Why E before every S?

    E makes the new ring; S shapes it. S on its own would resize the ring you already have and bend the wall below it. One E and one S: one new ring, exactly where you want it.

End of Part 2. Ctrl+S. (If you pressed Tab to look, press Tab again to go back to Edit Mode: the top is still selected.)

Part 3

The stem and the collar

Tools: the same four moves.

The stem narrows as it rises, in three rings; the collar is a thin wide disc at the top of it, the same trick as the base: out, up, back in.

  1. Start the stem

    The right half (3D view), keys only. The mouse can be anywhere over it; the typed number decides the size.

    Do this:

    1. a
      E, then straight away S 0.85 Enter. A flat step in.
    2. b
      E 0.15 Enter, then S 0.7 Enter. The start of the curve up into the stem.

    You should now see: a short slope rising out of the base.

  2. The stem

    The right half (3D view), keys only. The mouse can be anywhere over it; the typed number decides the size.

    Do this:

    1. a
      E 0.3 Enter, then S 0.76 Enter. Narrower again.
    2. b
      E 0.9 Enter, then S 0.74 Enter. The long thin part.

    You should now see: a stem 1.83 m up at its top, about 0.27 m from the middle to the edge there.

    Why three rings, not one?

    One long E and S would give a straight cone. Three rings, each narrowing a bit more slowly, bend the side into a curve, like the stem in the photo.

  3. The collar

    The right half (3D view), keys only. The mouse can be anywhere over it; the typed number decides the size.

    Do this:

    1. a
      E, then straight away S 2 Enter. A wide flat ledge: twice as wide as the stem top.
    2. b
      E 0.12 Enter. The collar’s rim, 0.12 m tall.
    3. c
      E, then straight away S 0.65 Enter. Step back in, ready for the head.

    You should now see: a thin disc sitting on the stem, a little wider than the head will be.

    Why such a big number?

    The stem top is thin: 0.27 m. Twice that is 0.55 m, a collar a bit wider than the head, as on a real pawn. S always works on the width it has now, so a big number is fine when the circle is small.

End of Part 3. Ctrl+S.

Part 4

The head

Tools: the same four moves, and M › At Center.

A ball made of rings: each ring is a slice of a sphere. In the bottom half each ring is higher and wider (S bigger than 1); in the top half higher and narrower (S smaller than 1); the last one closes into a point.

  1. The bottom half of the ball

    The right half (3D view), keys only. The mouse can be anywhere over it; the typed number decides the size.

    Do this:

    1. a
      E 0.16 Enter, then S 1.3 Enter.
    2. b
      E 0.19 Enter, then S 1.08 Enter. The widest ring: the middle of the ball, 0.5 m from the centre.

    You should now see: the lower half of a ball sitting on the collar.

  2. The top half

    The right half (3D view), keys only. The mouse can be anywhere over it; the typed number decides the size.

    Do this:

    1. a
      E 0.19 Enter, then S 0.92 Enter.
    2. b
      E 0.16 Enter, then S 0.77 Enter.
    3. c
      E 0.11 Enter, then S 0.54 Enter. A small circle at the very top.

    You should now see: a nearly round head with a small open-looking circle on top (it is still a face, selected).

    Why are the heights not all the same?

    Slices of a ball are close together near the middle (the side is steep) and spread out near the top and bottom (the side is flat). Equal heights would give a lumpy egg.

  3. Close the top

    The right half (3D view), keys only. The mouse can be anywhere over it; the typed number decides the size.

    Do this:

    1. a
      E 0.04 Enter. One last tiny ring.
    2. b
      M › At Center (the mouse over the right half): the whole top circle shrinks into one point.

    You should now see: a closed pawn, 2.8 m tall, with a point at the top of the head.

    Why not S 0?

    S 0 also squashes the circle to nothing, but leaves 32 corners stacked on top of each other. At Center merges them into one, which is clean.

End of Part 4. Ctrl+S.

Part 5

Finish and hand in

Tools: Tab, right-click › Shade Auto Smooth, the Material tab, Z.

Three short steps: smooth the curves, make it ivory, check it against the photo.

  1. Smooth it

    The right half: Tab, then right-click anywhere over the 3D view.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Tab: back to Object Mode. The pawn has an orange outline.
    2. b
      Right-click › Shade Auto Smooth.

    You should now see: the ball and the stem shade smoothly; the flat steps keep crisp edges.

    Why Auto Smooth, not Shade Smooth?

    Shade Smooth blurs every edge, and the flat steps would look melted. Auto Smooth smooths only where faces meet at less than 30°, so the curves go smooth and the steps stay sharp.

  2. Make it ivory

    The Properties editor (bottom right of the window) › the red sphere tab, Material. Then the 3D view.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Material tab › New.
    2. b
      Base Color › Hex F2E8D5 (ivory). Roughness 0.35.
    3. c
      Mouse over the 3D view: Z › Material Preview.

    You should now see: an ivory pawn, the colour of the one in the photo.

    Why does Solid shading stay grey?

    Solid shading shows the shape, not the material. Material Preview shows the colour and the shine.

  3. Compare and hand in

    The right half, then SEQTA.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Numpad 1: the pawn from the front, the same way the photo sees it. Compare: base, stem, collar, head.
    2. b
      Ctrl+S. Upload Lab12_Pawn_YourName.blend to SEQTA under Lab 12.

    You should now see: the same four parts as in the photo, in the same order and roughly the same proportions.

End of Section A.

Part 6

Section B (optional): a lamp post

Tools: everything above, used again.

Find a photo of a lamp post (an old street lamp works best: a wide base, a long column, rings, a lantern on top) and model it with the same moves. Load your photo the way Step 4 did, into the left half of a new file, Lab12_LampPost_YourName.blend.

One plan that works

Start exactly like Steps 6 to 8: a cylinder, Location Z 1, Tab, 2, Alt+click the top. Then, keeping the mouse over the 3D view:

  1. The plinth: G Z -1.6 Enter; E then S 0.8 Enter; E 0.3 Enter; S 0.85 Enter
  2. Up to the column: E then S 0.6 Enter; E 0.6 Enter; S 0.6 Enter; E then S 0.75 Enter
  3. The column: E 8 Enter; S 0.8 Enter
  4. A ring under the lamp: E then S 1.6 Enter; E 0.12 Enter; E then S 0.6 Enter; E 0.3 Enter
  5. The lamp: E then S 2.6 Enter; E 0.1 Enter; E 1 Enter; S 1.5 Enter
  6. The roof and the tip: E then S 1.25 Enter; E 0.35 Enter; S 0.3 Enter; E 0.3 Enter; S 0.4 Enter; E 0.1 Enter; M › At Center

Then Tab, right-click › Shade Auto Smooth, and a dark metal material (Base Color 2B3036, Metallic 0.6). Your photo will not match these numbers exactly: change them until your lamp post looks like your photo. That is the real skill.

Finished early? Pick one

A black pawn

Object Mode, click the pawn, Shift+D, then X 2.6 Enter: a copy one board square away. In the Material tab the material shows a 2 (two objects share it): click the 2 to give the copy its own, then Base Color 1E1714, Roughness 0.25. Now you have one of each.

Another piece from a photo

A bishop, a queen or a rook: find a photo, load it like Step 4, and build it ring by ring. A bishop’s head is an egg (more rings in the top half); a queen’s crown flares out (S bigger than 1 near the top); a rook’s top is a wide flat cylinder. Write your own numbers down as you go so you could build it again.

Smoother rings

Start again with the Add Cylinder panel’s Vertices set to 64 instead of 32. Every other number stays the same and the pawn comes out rounder. Why do the numbers not change?

Something’s not right

Find the problem that matches yours.

I can’t orbit (no middle mouse button)

Drag on the coloured gizmo at the top right of the 3D view to orbit. Or turn on Edit › Preferences › Input › Emulate 3 Button Mouse, then Alt + left-drag orbits.

I have no number pad (Numpad 1)

Use the 3D view’s View › Viewpoint › Front, or click the dull green circle (−Y) on the gizmo. Or turn on Edit › Preferences › Input › Emulate Numpad and use the 1 key at the top of the keyboard; but with that on, the 1, 2 and 3 keys change the view instead of the select mode, so in Step 8 click the Edge select button in the header instead of pressing 2.

The split went the wrong way (one half above the other)

You picked Horizontal Split. Hover the extra half: View › Area › Close Area. Then View › Area › Vertical Split.

File › Open does not show my photo

File › Open is for .blend files only. Use the Image Editor’s own Open button in its header (or Image › Open in the Image Editor, or Alt+O with the mouse over it).

The photo is huge, tiny, or off to one side

Hover the photo and press Home. Scroll to zoom it; middle-drag to slide it.

My keys do nothing, or the photo zooms instead

The mouse is over the left half. Every key goes to the half under the mouse: move it over the 3D view, then press the keys again.

Alt+click picked one line up the side, not the top

The click landed nearer a side edge than the top circle. Alt+click again, in the middle of the top face. Or press 3 (Face select), click the top face, then 2 to go back to Edge select.

G moved the whole cylinder, not just the top

You are in Object Mode (the header says Object Mode): Ctrl+Z, Tab, and do Step 8 again. Or everything was still selected in Edit Mode: Ctrl+Z, then Alt+click the top so only the top is orange.

S made it enormous or tiny

A typo: 92 instead of 0.92, or 0.092. Ctrl+Z and type it again. The number is “times as wide”, so it is always near 1 in this lab, except the collar’s 2.

A dark line round the pawn, or a ring that will not go anywhere

You pressed E and then Esc or right-click: the move was cancelled but the new ring stayed, sitting exactly on the old one. Ctrl+Z once more. (Or later: A to select everything, M › By Distance, which merges rings sitting on top of each other; then Alt+click the top again.)

I clicked somewhere and the top is not selected any more

Alt+click the top again (Edge select, middle of the top face). You can carry on from there: the moves only care about what is selected.

A ring went sideways or slanted

You moved the mouse and clicked before typing the number. Ctrl+Z. Press the key, type the number straight away, then Enter, without clicking.

M › At Center squashed the whole pawn into a point

Everything was selected, not just the top. Ctrl+Z, Alt+click the top (Edge select), then M › At Center again.

There is no Shade Auto Smooth

Blender is older than 4.1. Right-click › Shade Smooth, then in the Properties editor’s green triangle tab (Object Data) open Normals and tick Auto Smooth.

The pawn is still grey after Step 19

You are in Solid shading. Mouse over the 3D view, Z › Material Preview. Still grey? The material went on with the mouse over the wrong half or the pawn not selected: click the pawn and check the Material tab shows your material.

Eight quick questions

Pick an answer to lock it in. You’ll find out straight away whether you’re right.

1The top circle is 0.5 m from the middle. You press S, 0.8, Enter. How far is it now?

Right. S multiplies: 0.5 × 0.8 = 0.4 m.

Not quite. S multiplies the width it has now: 0.5 × 0.8 = 0.4 m.

2What does Z do after G?

Right. G moves, Z keeps the move on the up-and-down axis.

Not quite. Pressed during a move, Z locks it to the Z axis: straight up and down.

3You press E, then straight away S, 0.85, Enter. What do you get?

Right. The new ring stays at the same height and shrinks: a flat ledge.

Not quite. E makes a new ring; going straight to S means it never moves up, so shrinking it makes a flat step.

4After G, Z, -1.8, Enter on the top of a 2 m cylinder standing on the grid, how thick is the disc?

Right. The top drops from 2 m to 0.2 m.

Not quite. The top was at 2 m; moving it 1.8 m down leaves it at 0.2 m.

5Why must the mouse be over the right half while you type the moves?

Right. Over the photo, G or S would do Image Editor things instead.

Not quite. Every key goes to the area the mouse is over.

6In Edge select, what does Alt+click on the middle of the top face select?

Right. Alt+click selects a loop; with all its edges selected, the face inside is selected too.

Not quite. Alt+click selects a whole loop of edges; round the top that is the top circle, and the face inside comes with it.

7In the bottom half of the head the S numbers are above 1, in the top half below 1. Why?

Right. Widest in the middle, closing in above and below.

Not quite. Think of slicing a ball: the slices get wider up to the middle, then narrower.

8Why Shade Auto Smooth rather than Shade Smooth?

Right. Edges sharper than 30° stay sharp.

Not quite. Auto Smooth only smooths where faces meet at a gentle angle, so the ledges stay crisp.

Check yourself

Tick each one you can honestly do now. Anything left unticked is what to ask about next lesson.

Think about it

The pawn has 34 typed moves. If you wanted a pawn twice as tall but just as wide, which numbers would you change, and which would you leave alone? (Hint: one kind of move controls height, another controls width.)

Upload to SEQTA — Lab 12

Section A: Lab12_Pawn_YourName.blend with the finished pawn (smoothed, with its material). Section B, if you did it: Lab12_LampPost_YourName.blend.

Due one week from when this lab was handed out.

Teacher notes

Timing

Two lessons. Lesson 1: Parts 1 to 3 (set-up, base, stem and collar). Lesson 2: Parts 4 and 5 (head, finish), then Section B or the extensions. Part 1 is the slowest the first time: students who have done it before are through it in five minutes.

What changed from the handout

  • Every move has a number. The handout said “move it up a bit” and “scale it”; here each of the 34 moves is typed (G Z -1.8, E 0.15, S 0.7…), so every pawn comes out the same and a stuck student can be checked against the Ring builder and the checkpoints. The numbers were worked out from a Staunton pawn’s proportions and built in Blender to check them.
  • The top stays a closed face. The handout deleted the top edges (Step 19) and extruded the open rim, which left a hollow pawn with a hole in the head. Here the top face is extruded the whole way and closed with M › At Center: a solid, clean mesh, and one fewer technique to go wrong.
  • Image › Open, not File › Open. The handout’s Step 5 used File › Open, which opens .blend files. The photo now goes in through the Image Editor’s Open button.
  • The photo is supplied. A downloadable reference (a Blender render of the finished pawn on a board, photographed from the front) replaces the stock photo, so every student has the same picture and it matches the steps.
  • Splitting the window uses View › Area › Vertical Split; the corner drag from the handout is given as the alternative.
  • Finishing: Shade Auto Smooth and an ivory material were added so the result reads as a chess piece. The handout’s “Lab 11” in its Step 24 is Lab 12 throughout.
  • Section B (the lamp post) keeps the handout’s brief and adds one worked plan with numbers and a picture, for students who want a starting point.

Tested values

Every move was run in Blender 5.2.2 (bpy) exactly as written: after each move the height and radius of the selected ring were checked against the plan (all 34 match), and the finished mesh is closed (577 vertices, no holes). The checkpoint pictures and the reference photo were rendered from that file; the lamp post plan was built and checked the same way. Shade Auto Smooth needs Blender 4.1 or newer; on older versions use Shade Smooth plus Auto Smooth in Object Data › Normals (there is a fix for it).

Where students usually get stuck

Typing with the mouse over the photo (Steps 9 onwards). Alt+clicking near the side so a vertical edge gets selected (Step 8). Pressing Esc after E, which leaves a doubled ring (it shows as a dark line). Typing 92 for 0.92. Clicking in the viewport between moves and losing the selection. Using File › Open for the photo.

Quiz answers

1 0.4 m. 2 Locks the move to up and down. 3 A flat step in. 4 0.2 m. 5 Keys go to the area under the mouse. 6 The loop and the top face. 7 Ball slices widen to the middle, then narrow. 8 Smooths curves, keeps steps sharp.
